doc.title: Albert Murray interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 24, 1997

title: Innovation, built-in obsolescence and quality: cars and Japanese goods
summary: Murray uses the American automobile, Volkswagen, Japanese and Swiss quality to argue real innovation is quality and workmanship, and that hype sells bad music.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: You see? There’s a lot of things that save us with the American automobile, once they got to a certain point. In the beginning they wanted to be durable. This will be better than a horse because the horse is going to die. So they built the automobiles that lasted as long as they could make them last. And later on they realized they could saturate the market with it, so they went in for built-in obsolescence. But they had a problem there, which worked in the average man’s favor. And that is they had highway safety, do you see? So you couldn’t build a death trap simply because it wouldn’t last and it would fall apart. We’ve got laws to protect us against that. That’s a protection against advertising. Because advertising would sell anything, and people would change in it just when it started. So they went in for that. They had to make it safe, because there was laws against it. So they put the emphasis — the legal requirements for safety, and put the emphasis on the design so the car is still good and still working but the guy’s going to go buy another one because of the design. See that’s the way they got around built in obsolescence in an area where the public welfare became the determining factor. Because we were into that at the time that the Germans and the Europeans were in for durability you see? They started making better automobiles. I mean the Volkswagen put all these people at a disadvantage, see? So they had all these fancy designs and all of a sudden a bunch of people, for a number of years, they said this is just transportation. I’m just going to work and back, and I need to get there and back, so the Volkswagen is fine. The Japanese said heck we can beat them. Look at all that space they’re talking, there’s too many cars in all those American cities and they’re still making them bigger and bigger. They said we can get rid of that. It’s going to be durable, it’s going to be more reasonable in price, and that’s what happened. That’s what happened to the television, with high definition and all of that. I mean you go right to an American [inaudible], the biggest ever, they got SONYs in there. It’s SONY right in there with their monitors and so forth. The best quality is what they buy. So the Japanese beat them because they sold the whole propaganda thing there was they were selling it based on fluff. And the guys say, we’re going to base ours on efficiency. And all of a sudden, they were worried about the fact that all these people, so you go to Detroit to an auto factory, and these guys out there are making cars, but they’re all driving Japanese.
Do you think that the arts are —

But you see that’s the whole thing about that type of thing too, about innovation. So what turned out to be truly innovative was quality in automobile engines. You see what I mean? Delivered a good image at a reasonable price. So the guy who’s making the American automobile, in a lot of instances you see, couldn’t afford to buy it. So he’s buying a Japanese car to drive to work to make automobiles. Another guy could see that and said I should have one of those you see? Because the Japanese were selling quality. Workmanship. Like the Swiss. The Swiss have always sold expertise and workmanship. They can take half the amount of coal and oil you see — one boatload of oil and it would be billions of dollars of Swiss skill, because they could ship it back — how many watches could you get out of that? How many instruments could you get out of that you see? Whereas in Norway you’ve got to have these big slabs of steel to make these boats. And they’ve got all these itty bitty — one boatload of that would be worth two of the boats. It’s that type of thing that’s involved in innovation and so forth. You’ve got to look at the quality. In the arts it’s the same thing. But if you get marketing too closely, you could sell anything. You see that’s how a lot of times we got stuck with such terrible music as we have in the United States now. You don’t have to be a musician or to know music or to do anything. If the guy can sell it, if he can hype it, then he will turn that into the fad so all these people go running back because it’s the in thing. A year from now or two years from now, in a short time in any case, that’s gone. The guy’s got the money, he’s in something else. But he never was a musician, and this guy doesn’t need a musician anymore.
